918.title: Vatican II lived
918.hook: Mass in local languages, the priest facing the people, more of the Bible read aloud
918.howItsDone: Catholic parishes generally celebrate Mass in the local language with the priest facing the people and lay readers proclaiming the first readings; in some places the older Latin form is also celebrated with the bishop's permission.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Good Pope John, Angelo Roncalli, the farmer's son who wrote about peace. Your line was all people of goodwill. Did your message go out? Today, the council he called, seen from a pew. Day nine hundred eighteen.

Ask an older Catholic what Sunday Mass sounded like when they were small, and some will describe the same scene. The priest stood at an altar against the far wall, his back to the people. He prayed in Latin, much of it quietly. In the pews, some followed along in a missal with the translation printed beside it; others prayed the rosary on their own. Then, within a few years, the same parish changed. The priest turned around. He said The Lord be with you in English, or Spanish, or Tagalog. Lay people walked up to read. Bishops in Rome had met and written documents. This is the council in the pews.
screen: `THE PRIEST'S BACK, THE LATIN.` → `ROSARIES IN THE PEWS.` → `THEN HE TURNED AROUND.`

segments.voice: The Second Vatican Council's document on the liturgy is known by its opening Latin words, Sacrosanctum Concilium. Here is what it changed, and what it didn't. First, the language. The council allowed the Mass and the sacraments to be celebrated more widely in the people's own languages. Catholics sometimes hear Pentecost in that, when the crowd in Jerusalem was amazed, as Acts says in the Douay-Rheims, because "every man heard them speak in his own tongue." Second, the Bible. The document asks that the treasures of Scripture be opened up more richly, so that more of the Bible is read aloud at Mass. Third, the people. It speaks of the faithful taking part fully and actively, not as silent spectators. So lay people began to read, to sing the responses, to bring up the gifts. Fourth, the surprises. The document does not actually tell priests to turn the altar around; that came in the reforms that followed. And it does not abolish Latin. It says Latin is to be kept, and it gives Gregorian chant a place of honor. Catholics today still differ about all this. Some love the reformed Mass in their own language. Some are drawn to the older Latin form and attend it where it is allowed. And for some Catholics, Vatican II is not first a document at all. It is the Sunday the priest turned around.
screen: `THE PEOPLE'S OWN LANGUAGE.` · `MORE OF THE BIBLE, READ ALOUD.` · `TAKING PART, NOT WATCHING.` · `LATIN KEPT, ALTAR NOT ORDERED.` · then, large: `EVERY MAN HEARD THEM SPEAK IN HIS OWN TONGUE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: notice what changed in your parish. Settle, and breathe. Walk through a Mass you've been to, in your mind, or any church you've stood in. Where is the altar? Which way does the priest face? What language do you hear? Who walks up to read? Find one thing that the council touched, and one thing that stayed old: a hymn, a statue, a Latin word that survived. If you pray, you can pray for your parish as it is now. If you don't, simply hold that room in mind. The bell holds the time.
Sacrosanctum Concilium. The Second Vatican Council's document on the liturgy, which opened the Mass to people's own languages and asked the faithful to take part fully and actively.
Your line: the council in the pews. Today, ask someone who remembers the older Mass what changed for them, and just listen. Day nine hundred eighteen.

919.title: Paul VI (1963–1978)
919.hook: the pope who boarded planes to Jerusalem, India and New York, and told the United Nations no more war
919.howItsDone: Catholics keep the feast of Saint Paul VI, and the Holy See keeps a permanent observer at the United Nations, where later popes have also addressed the General Assembly.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Vatican II lived, under Sacrosanctum Concilium: the day the priest turned around. Your line was the council in the pews. What did you hear from someone who remembers? Today, the pope who carried that council to its end. Day nine hundred nineteen.

A thin man in white walks to a podium in New York. In front of him sit the representatives of the world's nations, in the hall of the United Nations General Assembly. He is the bishop of Rome, a long way from Rome. He came by plane. He has no army and no vote in this hall. He tells them he has nothing to ask for himself. Then, speaking in French, he says the words this day is built on. No more war. War never again. His name was Giovanni Battista Montini. As pope he was called Paul the Sixth.
screen: `A MAN IN WHITE IN NEW YORK.` → `NO ARMY, NOTHING TO ASK.` → `NO MORE WAR.`

segments.voice: Paul the Sixth came right after Good Pope John, and he is easy to overlook. Here are four ways in. First, the finisher. John called the council; Paul was elected between its sessions, with much of its work still ahead, and he brought it to its close and began putting it into practice. The Mass in local languages you remembered yesterday came in under him. Second, the traveler. He took the name of Paul, the apostle who crossed the sea again and again, and he got on airplanes. He went to Jerusalem and embraced the Orthodox patriarch Athenagoras there. He went to India. He went to New York. Third, the speech. At the United Nations he spoke of himself as an expert in humanity, a man with long experience of human beings, and he begged the nations: no more war, war never again. He told them that if they wanted to be brothers, they should let the weapons fall from their hands. Catholics hear in this the old promise in Isaiah, in the Douay-Rheims: "nation shall not lift up sword against nation, neither shall they be exercised any more to war." Fourth, the cost. Paul's years were not calm. Some of his teaching, especially his letter on marriage and birth control, was hard for some Catholics to accept, and it is still argued over. The Church has since named him a saint. What stays is a man without an army, standing in a hall of flags, asking the nations to put the weapons down.
screen: `THE POPE WHO FINISHED THE COUNCIL.` · `THE TRAVELER: JERUSALEM, INDIA, NEW YORK.` · `AT THE UN: NO MORE WAR.` · `A HARD PAPACY, A SAINT.` · then, large: `NATION SHALL NOT LIFT UP SWORD AGAINST NATION.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: hold the United Nations in mind. Settle, and breathe. Bring up that hall, the rows of desks, the name of each country on a card. Then the people behind the cards: diplomats who haven't slept, translators in their booths, peacekeepers far from home, staff who feed refugees. Pick one of them and stay with that person for a while. If you pray, you can pray for them, perhaps with Isaiah's line about swords. If you don't, simply hold them in mind and wish them steady hands. The bell holds the time.
Paul the Sixth. The pope who finished the council, traveled by plane, and told the nations at the UN: no more war.
Your line: no more war. Today, when a news story about a war crosses your screen, stop on it for one breath instead of scrolling past, and say the line. Day nine hundred nineteen.

920.title: Oscar Romero (1917–1980)
920.hook: an archbishop in El Salvador, shot while celebrating Mass, now honored as a saint
920.howItsDone: Catholics keep the feast of Saint Óscar Romero, and in El Salvador and elsewhere people gather where he died, at the hospital chapel in San Salvador, and at his tomb in the cathedral.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Paul the Sixth, a man in white before the nations. Your line was no more war. Which story did you stop on? Today, an archbishop in a country sliding toward war. Day nine hundred twenty.

Sunday morning in El Salvador, and in kitchens and market stalls, radios are tuned to the archdiocese's station. The archbishop is preaching from the cathedral, and he goes on a long time. He explains the readings. Then he does something sermons don't usually do. He reads the news of the week. The names of people killed. People taken from their homes and not seen again. A village where soldiers came. He reads them out so that they will be heard by someone. The man at the microphone was Óscar Romero.
screen: `RADIOS ON A SUNDAY.` → `A SERMON THAT READS THE NEWS.` → `THE NAMES, READ ALOUD.`

segments.voice: Romero's story turns four times. First, the quiet bishop. When he was made archbishop of San Salvador, he was known as a careful, bookish priest, and some expected him to keep his head down. Second, a friend's death. Soon after, his friend Rutilio Grande, a Jesuit priest who worked among poor farmers, was shot dead on a country road along with companions. Romero went to see the bodies and prayed over them that night. People who knew him say something changed in him there. Third, the voice. From then on he used his homilies, carried by radio, to name what was happening to his people, and he said the Church had to be the voice of those who had no voice. An old line in Proverbs, in the Douay-Rheims, sounds like his work: "Open thy mouth for the dumb." Dumb there means those who cannot speak. In his last Sunday homily he turned to the soldiers themselves. They were farmers' sons too, he reminded them, killing their own brothers and sisters, and he asked them, in God's name, to stop. Fourth, the altar. The next day he was celebrating Mass in the chapel of a hospital where he lived, and as he finished his homily a gunman shot him at the altar. The Church has since declared him a martyr and a saint, and he was canonized alongside yesterday's Paul the Sixth. Romero never ran for anything or carried a weapon. He was a bishop who read the Gospel on Sunday and then read out the names.
screen: `A CAREFUL, BOOKISH ARCHBISHOP.` · `A FRIEND KILLED ON A COUNTRY ROAD.` · `THE RADIO HOMILIES NAME THE DEAD.` · `SHOT AT THE ALTAR, NOW A SAINT.` · then, large: `OPEN THY MOUTH FOR THE DUMB.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: find one voice that isn't being heard. Settle, and breathe. Let someone come to mind whose story doesn't get told: a worker at the edge of your town, a neighbor who doesn't speak the language, someone in a place the news has forgotten. Say their situation to yourself in one plain sentence, the way Romero read the names. Then pick one small way to carry it after the bell: a call, a donation, a letter, telling their story to one person. If you pray, you can pray for them by name. The bell holds the time.
Oscar Romero. The archbishop of San Salvador who named his people's dead on the radio and was shot at the altar.
Your line: the voice of the voiceless. Today, do the one thing you chose, and say the name or the story out loud to someone. Day nine hundred twenty.

921.title: The four churchwomen (1980)
921.hook: Maura Clarke, Ita Ford, Dorothy Kazel and Jean Donovan, killed in El Salvador
921.howItsDone: Maryknoll, the Ursulines of Cleveland and parishes in El Salvador and the United States remember the four churchwomen with Masses and vigils, especially on the anniversary of their deaths.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Oscar Romero, who read the names of the dead on Sunday radio. Your line was the voice of the voiceless. Whose story did you carry? Today, four women in the same country. Day nine hundred twenty-one.

Two of them have just flown back from a meeting in Nicaragua. The other two have driven out to meet them, after dark, at the airport outside San Salvador, in a white van. Four American women: two Maryknoll sisters, an Ursuline sister and a young lay volunteer. They know the roads, the checkpoints, the risk. The van never reaches home. Days later, local people point the way to a shallow grave by a country road. Their names were Maura Clarke, Ita Ford, Dorothy Kazel and Jean Donovan.
screen: `A VAN LEAVES THE AIRPORT.` → `FOUR WOMEN, ONE ROAD.` → `IT NEVER REACHES HOME.`

segments.voice: It would be easy to tell this as a story about how they died. Their lives say more. First, who they were. Maura Clarke and Ita Ford were Maryknoll sisters, members of an American Catholic missionary order. Dorothy Kazel was an Ursuline sister from Cleveland. Jean Donovan was not a nun at all. She was a lay missionary, a young woman with a business career behind her, who had come to help. Second, what they did. In a country at war, they drove refugees to safety, brought food and medicine to families hiding from the fighting, and helped bury the dead. Ordinary work, done in a place where ordinary work had become dangerous. Third, the choice to stay. Friends and family asked them to come home. Jean Donovan wrote that she had thought about leaving, but couldn't bring herself to abandon the children she cared for. They knew what had happened to Romero. They stayed with the poor. Fourth, the truth told. Members of El Salvador's National Guard were later convicted of the killings, and questions about who gave the orders went on for years. Their families kept asking. Some Catholics read their story beside words Jesus speaks to his disciples at the Last Supper, in John's Gospel, in the Douay-Rheims: "But I have called you friends." Just before it, he says he will no longer call them servants. Not servants. Friends. These women had not gone to El Salvador to die. They had gone to be with people, and when staying became dangerous, they kept being with them.
screen: `THREE SISTERS AND A VOLUNTEER.` · `REFUGEES, FOOD, BURIALS.` · `ASKED TO LEAVE, THEY STAYED.` · `THE KILLERS CONVICTED, QUESTIONS REMAIN.` · then, large: `BUT I HAVE CALLED YOU FRIENDS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: hold missionaries in mind. Settle, and breathe. Picture someone far from home tonight because they chose to be with people who need help: a sister in a clinic, a volunteer at a border, a lay worker in a refugee camp, a doctor in a war zone. You don't need a name. Notice what their day might hold: a long drive, a checkpoint, a child who needs medicine. If you pray, you can pray for missionaries, and for the people they stay with. If you don't, simply hold them in mind and wish them safe roads. The bell holds the time.
Jean Donovan. The lay missionary among the four churchwomen killed in El Salvador, who wrote that she couldn't bring herself to abandon the children she cared for.
Your line: they stayed with the poor. Today, stay a little longer with someone you'd usually hurry past. Day nine hundred twenty-one.

922.title: The Missionaries of Charity (1950)
922.hook: the sisters in white and blue saris, begun by Teresa of Calcutta, who care for the dying
922.howItsDone: Missionaries of Charity sisters, in their white saris with blue borders, run homes for the dying, the abandoned and the sick in many countries, and volunteers of any faith or none can often come to help with the daily washing, feeding and cleaning.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the four churchwomen, among them Jean Donovan, who were asked to come home and didn't. Your line was they stayed with the poor. Who did you stay a little longer with? Today, sisters whose whole work is staying. Day nine hundred twenty-two.

A long room in Kolkata, beside a Hindu temple. Rows of low beds. On each, someone who was found on the street, too sick to walk. A sister in a white sari with blue stripes kneels at one of them with a basin of water. She is washing a man's feet. He may not live through the week, and she knows it. She is not there to cure him. She is there so that he does not die alone, unwashed, unnamed. The house is called Nirmal Hriday. The sisters are the Missionaries of Charity.
screen: `A LONG ROOM IN KOLKATA.` → `A SISTER WITH A BASIN.` → `SO NO ONE DIES ALONE.`

segments.voice: The order was begun by the woman Catholics now call Saint Teresa of Calcutta, Mother Teresa, a teacher who left her convent school to live among the poorest people of the city. Four things to know. First, the promise. Like other sisters, they make vows of poverty, chastity and obedience. Their rule adds one more promise: wholehearted and free service to the poorest of the poor. Free means no payment, ever. Second, the thirst. In their chapels, beside the crucifix, the sisters put two words from the cross in John's Gospel. In the Douay-Rheims: "I thirst." The sisters hear in them Jesus thirsting for love, and they see him in the person on the bed. Third, the work, spread wide. The order grew far beyond Kolkata: homes for the dying, for abandoned children, for people with leprosy, for people with AIDS, soup kitchens in big Western cities. There are brothers and priests in the same family now too. The work is plain: washing, feeding, sitting, holding a hand. Fourth, the questions. Not everyone has praised it. Some critics, including doctors who visited, questioned the standard of medical care in the homes. Supporters answer that the homes were meant for comfort and presence at the end, not for hospital treatment. Both are part of the honest story. Today's line comes from a British journalist who filmed the sisters. He called his book Something Beautiful for God, after a phrase tradition links with Mother Teresa. Not something impressive. Something beautiful, like a clean bed and a held hand.
screen: `A TEACHER LEAVES HER SCHOOL.` · `FREE SERVICE TO THE POOREST.` · `I THIRST, BESIDE THE CROSS.` · `PRAISED, AND QUESTIONED.` · then, large: `I THIRST.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: hold someone who is dying, or very ill, in mind. Settle, and breathe. It might be a grandparent, a friend in a hospice, a neighbor you haven't seen in months, or a stranger in a hospital you passed. Picture their room. Picture someone sitting with them. Then ask, gently, whether that someone could be you: a visit, a phone call, a card, an hour of sitting. If you pray, you can pray for them, and for the people who care for the dying. If you don't, simply hold them in mind. The bell holds the time.
Nirmal Hriday. The house in Kolkata where the Missionaries of Charity cared for the dying, so that no one died alone, unwashed or unnamed.
Your line: something beautiful. Today, if you can, make that visit or that call. If you can't, do one plain, unseen kindness for someone who can't repay it. Day nine hundred twenty-two.

923.title: John Paul II (1978–2005)
923.hook: a pope from Poland who opened his papacy crying be not afraid
923.howItsDone: Catholics keep the feast of Saint John Paul II, and his words be not afraid are often sung, printed on banners, and quoted at confirmations and youth gatherings.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Missionaries of Charity at Nirmal Hriday, a basin of water and a held hand. Your line was something beautiful. What plain kindness did you do? Today, a pope from Poland. Day nine hundred twenty-three.

Saint Peter's Square, packed. The new pope stands before the crowd at the Mass that begins his papacy. He is broad-shouldered, a former actor with a voice that carries. He comes from a country behind the Iron Curtain, under a communist government wary of the Church. And partway through his homily he says it, then says it again: be not afraid. Open wide the doors for Christ. Open the borders of states, of economic and political systems. Do not be afraid. His name was Karol Wojtyła. He took the name John Paul.
screen: `A NEW POPE, A FULL SQUARE.` → `FROM BEHIND THE IRON CURTAIN.` → `BE NOT AFRAID.`

segments.voice: Those words were not a slogan dreamed up on the day. They came out of a life. Four pieces of it. First, loss. Karol grew up in a small Polish town, and by the time he was a young man his mother, his only brother and his father had all died. He knew grief early. Second, the occupation. When Nazi Germany occupied Poland, the universities were shut. He worked in a stone quarry and a chemical plant, acted in an underground theater that performed in people's living rooms, and studied for the priesthood in a secret seminary. All of it could have cost him his life. Third, the long middle. As priest and then archbishop of Kraków, under a communist government, he hiked and skied and kayaked with students, taught philosophy, and pushed for churches the state didn't want built. Fourth, the words. So when he said be not afraid, he was speaking as someone who had been afraid with good reason, and had gone on anyway. The words belong to the Gospels first. When the disciples see Jesus walking toward them on the water at night and cry out in terror, he says, in the Douay-Rheims: "Be of good heart: it is I, fear ye not." John Paul's papacy was long and sometimes argued over, and the coming days look at a few of its moments. But the opening note was this one: the fear is real, and the voice on the water speaks to it anyway.
screen: `A CHILDHOOD OF LOSS.` · `QUARRY, SECRET THEATER, SECRET SEMINARY.` · `A PRIEST UNDER COMMUNISM.` · `THE WORDS COME FROM THE WATER.` · then, large: `BE OF GOOD HEART: IT IS I, FEAR YE NOT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: find one brave thing. Settle, and breathe. Let one thing come to mind that you've been putting off because it scares you. Not a grand thing. A conversation you're avoiding. An apology. A doctor's appointment. Saying no. Saying yes. Hold it, and notice where the fear sits in your body. Breathe there. Then shrink the brave thing down to its first step, small enough to take today. If you pray, you can pray the line from the water: be of good heart, fear ye not. The bell holds the time.
Karol Wojtyła. The Polish pope who had lived through occupation, grief and an underground seminary, and who became John Paul the Second.
Your line: be not afraid. Today, take that first small step, and when the fear shows up, say the line under your breath. Day nine hundred twenty-three.

924.title: Solidarity
924.hook: John Paul II's visits home to Poland and a peaceful workers' movement that changed the country
924.howItsDone: In Gdańsk, a monument to the shipyard workers stands at the gate where the strike began, and Polish Catholics visit the grave of Blessed Jerzy Popiełuszko at his Warsaw parish.

segments.voice: Yesterday, John Paul the Second, Karol Wojtyła: a quarry, a secret theater, and a new pope saying be not afraid. Your line was be not afraid. What first small step did you take? Today, what happened when he went home. Day nine hundred twenty-four.

A gate at a shipyard on the Baltic coast of Poland. The workers inside are on strike, and they have locked themselves in. On the gate, people have hung flowers, a picture of the Virgin Mary, and a photograph of the Polish pope. Outside, families pass food through the bars. Inside, a priest hears confessions in the open yard, and the strikers kneel on the concrete for Mass. The strike leader is an electrician with a big mustache named Lech Wałęsa. The movement being born on that dock will be called Solidarity.
screen: `A SHIPYARD GATE ON THE BALTIC.` → `FLOWERS, MARY, THE POPE.` → `MASS ON THE CONCRETE.`

segments.voice: Solidarity's story has four turns. First, the visit. Not long after he became pope, John Paul went home to Poland, then under a communist government. Enormous crowds came out. In Warsaw he prayed aloud that the Spirit would come down and renew the face of the earth, and then he added: the face of this land. He was borrowing a psalm. In the Douay-Rheims it reads: "thou shalt renew the face of the earth." Some who were there say people looked around at the crowd and realized how many of them there were. Second, the strike. At the shipyard in Gdańsk, workers struck, and out of the strikes came Solidarity, a trade union the government did not control. Its badge became a word painted in tumbling red letters. Third, the hard years. The government declared martial law, banned the union, and jailed its leaders. Solidarity went underground. A young priest in Warsaw, Jerzy Popiełuszko, held Masses for the country and preached a line from Saint Paul, in the Douay-Rheims: "overcome evil by good." The secret police murdered him. His funeral became a sea of people, and still the movement did not turn to violence. Fourth, the end. In time the government sat down with Solidarity at a round table and agreed to partly free elections, and Solidarity's candidates swept the seats open to them. Communist rule in Poland ended without a civil war. Some historians link the movement to the wider changes that soon followed across Eastern Europe. Catholic teaching calls solidarity a virtue: a firm commitment to the good of every person, because we are all responsible for all. In Poland, it was also a union card.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: stand with workers, in your mind first. Settle, and breathe. Think back over the last day and count the people who worked so your life could run: whoever picked the food you ate, drove the truck, cleaned the building, answered the phone, stocked the shelf. Pick one face, real or imagined, and stay with it. What is their shift like? What would make it fairer? If you pray, you can pray for workers, using Paul's line: overcome evil by good. If you don't, simply hold them in mind with gratitude. The bell holds the time.
Solidarity. The Polish workers' union born in the Gdańsk shipyard, and a Catholic virtue: a firm commitment to the good of all.

Your line: without violence. This week ran from Vatican II in the pews, through Paul the Sixth, Romero, the four churchwomen, the Missionaries of Charity and John Paul, to Solidarity. Today, thank one worker by name. Day nine hundred twenty-four.

fork.setup: you're a Solidarity leader. the union is banned and a priest who preached for you has been murdered. what do you do?
options: fight back with weapons.
keep going underground, without violence.
give up and join the government.
fork.reveal: the movement kept going underground, without violence, until the government came to the round table.
